The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and serves the emotional arc of the narrative. The author stretches time during the protagonist's initial weekend visit, lingering on sensory details, meals, and quiet porch conversations to mirror the slow, deliberate pace of the mother's small-town life. Conversely, time is effectively compressed during the four-hour train rides and the weeks between the visit and the phone call from Doris ("A month is not a long time. It is the length of a billing cycle."). Finally, time slows down and stretches once again when the narrator returns to the empty house alone, allowing the reader to sit with the character's profound realization about his mother's love and mortality.
